newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian party fracture seen aiding ruling party.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian party fracture seen aiding ruling party.

text.p: A vicious battle within the minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) ahead of general elections in May is expected ultimately to benefit the ruling Golkar party in the polls, analysts said on Sunday.

More than six months after PDI leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted by a government-backed rival at a special party congress, conflict in the party's historically unstable fusion of Christian and Nationalist forces continues to spill onto the streets.

Last week, thousands of Megawati supporters protested on Java and Sumatra, marching on offices of the government election body, the General Election Institute (LPU), in a number of big cities, including the capital Jakarta.

At the same time, Megawati's numerous backers continue to pursue civil legal action against party members who attended the June conference in the north Sumatran city of Medan, which elected deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi.
"If the instability in the PDI shies away voters, then these voters would be logically voting for Golkar," said Marzuki Darusman, vice-chairman of the official national human rights commission.

He argued that under normal circumstances PDI voters would be more attracted to Golkar because both parties are "open and nationalist", where the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) is ideologically exclusive and built on religious lines.
Only these three parties are sanctioned by the government to contest the May 29 poll.
However, with four major riots in the past six months showing growing frustration in the community, Darusman said this dissatisfaction could be the "wild card" at election time.
"The factor of dissatisfaction and to what extent this will channel votes to the PPP as a matter of protest is another question," Darusman told Reuters.
Other analysts say voter attendance and the percentage of deliberately spoiled votes, known as the Golput or "white group" movement, will indicate public anger with the government.
However, some diplomats say tight control of the election right down to the village level will mask any popular dissent.

Political analysts say Megawati must compromise and rejoin the PDI under Surjadi's leadership, but in an unusually strongly worded speech on Friday she maintained that she was the only legal PDI leader.

"Once again, I want to stress that the only PDI which is entitled to join the general election in 1997 is the one elected for the period of 1993-1998," Megawati told hundreds of supporters at her Jakarta home.
"It is not another PDI and also not the PDI under the name of anyone else," she said on the party's 24th anniversary.

Surjadi held his anniversary celebration at a remote tourist resort in Central Sulawesi along with Armed Forces Chief General Fiesal Tanjung, who threatened "action would taken" if Megawati held a rival birthday party. There was no confrontation.

The government, which has said it only recognises Surjadi's leadership, has backed the decision of the LPU to only list Surjadi's candidates. The decision to reject an alternate list from Megawati's camp is subject to a legal challenge.
Megawati accused the government in her Friday speech of meddling in the PDI for all of its 24 years.
Surjadi, who Megawati replaced as party leader in 1993, also made accusations of interference: "The internal conflicts of PDI are just being exploited."
Diplomatic sources said it appeared the government had no great commitment to Surjadi as PDI leader and this was shown by the low-key handling of demonstrations by Megawati supporters.
In one such demonstration Megawati backers painted graffiti on Surjadi's official residence as police and soldiers watched.

"The government appears to be quite happy for the PDI factions to remain at loggerheads and they see Surjadi's inability to unite the party as a plus factor that could only benefit the ruling Golkar in the May 29 elections," a senior diplomat said.
